Common questions and mistakes
1. Why K ij ∗ f ? Because the PDE gives u = Γ ∗ f and differentiating twice yields D ij u = ( D ij Γ) ∗ f
as distributions. Section 3 explains each implication.
2. Is i = j permitted in the cancellation formula? Yes. Off-diagonal cancellation follows by
reflection; diagonal cancellation follows because the average of θ 2
i is 1 /n . See the proof of ( 4.4 ).
3. Is D ij Γ = K ij everywhere? Only away from zero. Distributionally, D ij Γ = p . v . K ij − δ ij δ 0 /n .
4. Why does the diagonal formula contain − f/n but the mixed formula not? Precisely
because δ ij = 1 for i = j and 0 otherwise in ( 4.7 ).
5. Why can we subtract f ( x ) under the integral? Each truncated centered annulus has zero
integral against K ij , so the subtracted constant contributes nothing. The difference f ( x − z ) − f ( x )
gains a factor | z | .
6. Why does p = 2 look easier? Plancherel turns derivatives into multiplication by powers of ξ ,
and P

7. Why is the bad part mean zero? The dyadic decomposition subtracts each cube’s average,
which is the precise cancellation needed for the kernel-difference estimate.
8. Why retain ∥ u ∥ p in interior estimates? A nonzero harmonic function can have ∆ u = 0 and
D 2 u ̸ = 0 inside a bounded region.
